passage:
Jahnavi: ok so someone in the canteen said my lunch "smells weird" and that my kurta looks "so costume-y" 😠
Rafiq: WHAT. who?
Jahnavi: some guy called Callum. Everyone kind of laughed. I froze. I felt about two inches tall
Rafiq: I'm so sorry. what did you do?
Jahnavi: after a minute I said "It's my lunch, and it's really good." then I picked up my tray and moved to the window table. Ana from the lab came with me
Rafiq: good for you 👍
Jahnavi: honestly for one second I thought I'd just eat in the stairwell from now on
Rafiq: no way. bring the same lunch tomorrow, I'll sit with you
Jahnavi: ok 🙂 I'll bring extra. and I'm wearing the kurta again

qa.q: Who moved to the window table with Jahnavi?
qa.a: Ana from the lab moved with Jahnavi.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel after the remark in the canteen?
qa.a: Small and angry: Jahnavi wrote about feeling about two inches tall and sent an angry face.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do that was a good way to respond?
qa.a: Jahnavi answered calmly that it was a good lunch, then walked to another table with an ally and stayed proud of the kurta and the food.

qa.q: How might Callum have seen the comment?
qa.a: Callum may have meant it as a joke, since others laughed, without noticing how belittling it felt to Jahnavi.

grounding: Someone sneers at the protagonist's food and dress; the protagonist feels small and angry, answers calmly, seeks allies and stays proud of the background.

passage: Tenzin had done everything that was expected: finished his degree, passed the bank exam, come home to the hill town with a steady job and a scarf from his mother. And now, on the evening bus back from the branch, he thought, is this it? The mountains looked the same as ever. At night he scrolled for hours until his eyes stung, and woke up feeling as though nothing had happened at all. On Sunday Binita, who ran the little village library from her verandah, asked him to help read stories to eight children who couldn't yet manage on their own. He said he was rubbish at it. He went anyway. The children argued over the yak story. Tenzin laughed properly for the first time in weeks, then wondered what else he might try.

qa.q: Where did Binita run the little library?
qa.a: Binita ran it from her verandah.

qa.q: What was Tenzin worried about on the bus home?
qa.a: Tenzin was worried that this steady job might be all there was, and unsure what it was all for.

qa.q: What small step helped Tenzin begin to find direction?
qa.a: He tried helping Binita read stories to children, which led him to laugh and wonder what else to try.

qa.q: How might Binita see Tenzin's reluctance to help?
qa.a: Binita probably sees it as ordinary self-doubt, and invited him because trying something is how purpose starts.

grounding: After doing what he was supposed to do, the protagonist feels empty and numbs with scrolling; a small experiment of helping others opens a path.

passage: Ira stared at the biology notes she had highlighted in three colours, and felt like a fraud. Her parents had wanted her to be a doctor since she was seven, and everyone in the lane knew. Her father had a photo of a white coat framed above the radio. But the only thing she did well after class was draw the tea stall and its regulars. Pema, the art teacher at the school, said one afternoon, "Tell them what you love, Ira. They can't guess." At dinner she put down her spoon. "Papa, Mummy, I want to study design. I'll finish my degree first, and if it doesn't work in two years, I'll take the exam again." Her mother's eyes filled. Her father was silent for a long time. "We're worried," he finally said. "We'll think." Ira nodded. It wasn't a yes, but it was true.

qa.q: What did Ira's father have framed above the radio?
qa.a: He had a photo of a white coat framed above the radio.

qa.q: Why did Ira feel like a fraud?
qa.a: She was working towards her parents' dream of becoming a doctor when what she really loved was drawing.

qa.q: What did Ira do that was wise at dinner?
qa.a: She said honestly what she loves and offered a path with a fallback, and accepted her parents' worry.

qa.q: How might Ira's parents see her news?
qa.a: As a frightening change to a dream they have held for years, since her mother's eyes filled and her father was silent.

grounding: The parents' dream is not hers and she feels like a fraud; she tells them what she loves, proposes a path with a fallback and accepts their worry.

passage: Vaibhav here. Let me tell you what I noticed about Yamini after placement results came out. She was in the canteen with her phone held close, scrolling through everyone's announcements. "Everyone knows exactly what they want," she said to nobody in particular, and pushed her plate away. I couldn't tell if she was sad or just tired. She didn't apply for the same internships as the others. She went quiet for a few days. Then I saw her sign up for a one-day science outreach at a nearby school, just to see what it was like. She came back talking about the students' questions. A week later, over tea, I admitted I'd chosen my own internship mostly because my roommate had. Yamini just stared at me. "You? Really?" Then she laughed for the first time in days.

qa.q: What was Yamini looking at on her phone in the canteen?
qa.a: She was scrolling through everyone's placement announcements.

qa.q: What might Yamini have been feeling when she said everyone knows exactly what they want?
qa.a: Possibly behind and envious, since she pushed her plate away, though Vaibhav says it was hard to tell if Yamini was sad or just tired.

qa.q: What did Yamini do that was a useful way to handle the feeling?
qa.a: She tried something that interested her, a one-day outreach at a school, instead of only comparing herself with others.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's confession have changed things for Yamini?
qa.a: It showed her that others are also guessing, which was a relief, so she laughed for the first time in days.

grounding: Friends seem to know what they want and the protagonist feels behind; trying things and learning others are guessing too eases the envy.

passage: I'm Naina, and I was sitting next to Madhuri at my aunt's engagement lunch when Madhuri turned to the woman across the table, Gurpreet, with a notebook already open. "Aunty, how did you find your direction?" Gurpreet laughed. "Find? I changed course three times. First chemistry, then six years of teaching, then a small print shop, and now I train apprentices." Madhuri leaned forward, so intent that her dal went cold. "So there's no formula?" "Not one that I found." I couldn't tell whether Madhuri was disappointed or relieved. She was quiet on the drive home. But later I saw the notebook page: she'd written "collect stories, not formulas", underlined twice. Next week she signed up for a short course she'd been avoiding, just to see what it felt like.

qa.q: How many times did Gurpreet say she changed course?
qa.a: Gurpreet said she changed course three times.

qa.q: What might Madhuri have been feeling about Gurpreet's answer?
qa.a: Curious and possibly a mix of disappointment and relief, as Madhuri leaned forward intently, though Naina says Naina could not tell.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do with the answer that was helpful?
qa.a: Madhuri wrote down "collect stories, not formulas" and tried a short course instead of waiting for certainty.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see the question from a young person?
qa.a: As a chance to share honestly, since Gurpreet laughed and told the real, winding story rather than a tidy plan.

grounding: The protagonist asks an older woman how she found direction; she changed course three times, and the protagonist collects stories and starts trying things.

passage: It was festival week and the hostel corridor thumped with drums until midnight, with an exam in five days. Sarika sat on her bed with her grandmother's small book of verses, reading the same page for the third time. Something in one line made her stop. For a week she got up early, in the little quiet before the drums, and read a verse and sat still. It comforted her. But she noticed how tempting it was to copy an answer down whole and stop asking. On Saturday she took the book to Irawati Tai, the warden's elderly aunt who ran a study circle. "What do you think this line means?" asked Irawati Tai, instead of explaining. Sarika hesitated. "I'm not sure. Part of it makes me uneasy." "Good," said Irawati Tai. "Bring that too."

qa.q: How many days were left before Sarika's exam?
qa.a: Five days.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel about turning to the verses?
qa.a: Comforted by them, but wary of how tempting it was to copy an answer down whole and stop asking.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that was wise?
qa.a: She let the verses comfort her and also took them to Irawati Tai to discuss, including the parts that made her uneasy.

qa.q: How might Irawati Tai see Sarika's unease with the line?
qa.a: As a useful sign of real thinking, since Irawati Tai said "Good" and asked her to bring that too.

grounding: The protagonist turns to a book of verses for meaning and lets it comfort her while questioning and discussing it with others, not taking a ready-made answer.

passage: Gargi here, Harsha's roommate. I'm writing this down because I'm not sure what I'm seeing. For three weeks Harsha has slept until noon, skipped lunch, and said things like "I'm just lazy" and "I've wasted my whole youth." Harsha says it flatly, without expecting a reply. I can't know what's going on inside. It could be exhaustion, it could be worry about something. On Tuesday I said, "Lazy people don't sit up at night feeling this bad." Harsha half smiled. I suggested one tiny step: shower, then walk to the gate and back. Harsha did, and afterwards ate half a sandwich. I also said if it keeps going, the college counsellor is worth seeing, and I'd go along to the door. Harsha said maybe, and it is a maybe I'll ask about again on Friday.

qa.q: How long had Harsha been sleeping until noon and skipping lunch?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling, given the flat words about being lazy?
qa.a: Harsha may be feeling low and hopeless, saying flatly "I'm just lazy" and "I've wasted my whole youth", though Gargi says the reason inside cannot be known.

qa.q: What small step did Gargi suggest, and what could follow?
qa.a: A shower and a walk to the gate and back, and if it keeps going, a visit to the college counsellor.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel while watching Harsha these three weeks?
qa.a: Gargi seems worried but careful, writing things down instead of guessing what is inside Harsha, and planning to ask about the counsellor again on Friday.

grounding: The protagonist labels the self lazy and directionless and thinks youth is wasted; a friend meets it with kindness, one tiny step and a suggestion of help.

passage:
Trisha: I can't stop hearing this voice. It says you're worthless
Deepika: Oh Trish. What happened?
Trisha: I forgot to upload our group's final file. The deadline passed. Three of us lost marks because of me
Deepika: That's a serious mistake. It's also one mistake. The voice is shame, not a fact about you
Trisha: It feels like a fact
Deepika: I know. What would you say to me if I'd done it?
Trisha: That I'd messed up and could still fix it
Deepika: So say that to yourself
Trisha: ...ok. I'll write to the professor tonight and explain, and tell the other two myself first
Deepika: I'll sit with you while you write it

qa.q: What did Trisha forget to do?
qa.a: Trisha forgot to upload the group's final file.

qa.q: What is Trisha feeling as the voice keeps repeating itself?
qa.a: Deep shame, since the voice saying worthless feels like a fact.

qa.q: What did Trisha decide to do about the mistake?
qa.a: Trisha decided to tell the other two directly first and then write to the professor to explain, which owns the harm and repairs it.

qa.q: How might the two teammates feel when Trisha tells them directly?
qa.a: They may feel disappointed about the marks, but respected for being told directly rather than finding out later.

grounding: After a serious mistake the protagonist hears a voice saying worthless; with a friend the mistake is separated from the self, the harm is owned and a repair is planned.

passage:
Monday. Ramesh forgot to return Yamini's notes before her exam, and she had to borrow a classmate's at the last minute. "I'm useless," he told the ceiling that night. The words felt heavy and no use to anyone.
Thursday. In the hostel washroom mirror he tried a different sentence, aloud: "I made a mistake, and I am still a person worth respect." It felt odd. Then he went to find Yamini. "I was careless and it cost you. I'm sorry. Here are the notes and a set of my own copies." She nodded. "Thanks for saying it straight."
Two weeks later. Ramesh caught himself about to be late again with a borrowed book and set a phone reminder instead of just feeling bad about it.

qa.q: Whose notes did Ramesh forget to return before the exam?
qa.a: Yamini's notes.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh say the new sentence to the mirror?
qa.a: He wanted to stop calling himself useless, and to treat himself as someone worth respect while still owning the mistake.

qa.q: What made Ramesh's self-kindness real accountability rather than an excuse?
qa.a: He apologised plainly, brought the notes and copies, and later set a reminder so the mistake would not repeat.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Ramesh apologised plainly?
qa.a: Probably relieved and respected, since she thanked him for saying it straight.

grounding: The protagonist learns to say he made a mistake and is still worth respect; self-compassion makes it easier to apologise, repair and change.

passage: Dev here. I share a room with Yusuf, so I saw this. Last week Yusuf forwarded a private message of Reena's to the class group chat. Reena found out and stopped speaking to him. On Tuesday Reena caught up with him at the stairs and I heard her say, "I forgive you." Yusuf's shoulders dropped, his eyes went wet, and he stood there. Then he said, "I don't think I deserve that." I can't tell whether he felt relief, shame, or both. Reena said, "You don't have to earn it today. Just don't do it again." He didn't ask her for anything more. That evening he deleted the message from the group, said sorry to the class, and now checks with people before he shares anything of theirs.

qa.q: Where did Reena tell Yusuf she forgave him?
qa.a: At the stairs.

qa.q: What might Yusuf have been feeling when he said he didn't deserve forgiveness?
qa.a: Possibly relief and shame at once, since his shoulders dropped and his eyes went wet, though Dev says Dev cannot tell for sure.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do after being forgiven that showed he took it seriously?
qa.a: He deleted the message, apologised to the class and began checking with people before sharing anything of theirs, without asking Reena for more.

qa.q: How might Reena see the moment on the stairs?
qa.a: As a choice to forgive that does not erase the harm, since she told him not to do it again.

grounding: The person who was hurt says she forgives the protagonist, who feels relief and unworthiness, accepts it humbly and changes his behaviour.
